%%
%% The abstract is a short summary of the work to be presented in the
%% article.
\begin{abstract}
The basic theory of threads and locks in separation logic is well understood. However, locks as they are actually implemented have further variations and subtleties, including restrictions on transferring locks between threads, recursive mutexes, and classes designed for RAII patterns. In this paper, we present separation logic specifications for the C++ mutex library in the BRiCk logic. We identify and abstract out common patterns, including a mechanism for tracking a thread's mutex ownership, which can be used to enforce the mutex library's requirements. We demonstrate that our specifications are satisfied by implementations that explicitly track and check the owning thread, and thus do not satisfy the standard separation logic specifications for locks. We also show in a case study that our tracking logic is modular, so that even though mutexes require thread-specific predicates, the fact that a class uses a mutex internally can be hidden from the class's clients. %qualify a little -- we do need my_mutexes
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Mechanized concurrent separation logic (CSL) tools, such as those built in the Iris framework~\cite{iris}, can now verify code written in real languages. Logics like VST~\cite{vst}, BRiCk~\cite{brick}, and RustBelt~\cite{rustbelt} give Hoare rules for a large subset of C, Rust, and C++. However, specification of language features alone is not enough to verify real code. Most languages ship with extensive standard libraries, and programmers treat these libraries as if they were language primitives. This makes standard libraries a high-value target for specification and verification: they usually have only one or a few implementations and are used in almost all other code in the language. C++'s concurrency support library, for example, provides threads, atomic operations, mutexes/locks, and futures, and is the standard way to write portable concurrent programs. Threads, atomics, and locks have been thoroughly studied in concurrent separation logic, but C++'s locks include some restrictions and variants that have not previously been formalized.

First, unlike the standard separation-logic treatment of locks, C++ mutex operations place restrictions on which threads can perform them and whether they are currently held. For instance, the basic \lstinline{std::mutex} class must be released by the same thread that acquired it, cannot be acquired twice by the same thread, and must not be held when deallocated. One might expect that a thread acquiring a lock twice would be deadlocked but safe, but in fact violating any of these conditions is \emph{undefined behavior}, meaning that it could lead to unsafe behavior and must not occur in verified code\kedu{should be avoided (I know we said "in verified code", but people who rely on implementation dependent behavior might have a different take on "must not occur"...) }\wm{Pretty sure it's UB specifically because it crashes the standard Pthread mutex implementation.}. We develop a general mechanism for tracking a thread's lock ownership, based on a reusable ghost state pattern, and use it to enforce the standard library's restrictions. In keeping with the OO\kedu{Object-Oriented (use full name for the first appearance?)} principle of encapsulation, when an object uses a mutex in a well-structured way, tracking predicates need not appear in the object's representation predicate, allowing it to be transferred freely between threads as in conventional CSL.

Second, the standard library includes three main variants of mutexes\footnote{The library also includes timed variants of each mutex type, on which attempts to acquire may time out, but from the partial-correctness perspective these are identical to the non-timed variants.}: ordinary mutex, recursive mutex, and shared mutex (i.e., reader-writer lock). Recursive mutexes, which can be acquired multiple times by a single thread, have not previously been formalized in separation logic, but are widely used in object-oriented programming---they allow a thread-safe method to acquire a lock on its object's contents even if it can be called from within another thread-safe method. We give specifications for all three variants, including a specification of recursive mutexes that allows generic reasoning over whether the lock is already held.

Finally, the standard library includes a collection of mutex container classes following the Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII) pattern, where a resource (in this case, a mutex) is acquired when the container is created and released when it is destroyed. These classes are generic in the underlying type of mutex, using C++'s \emph{named requirement} feature (similar to \emph{interfaces} in other OO languages): the underlying mutex need only meet the \lstinline{BasicLockable} named requirement, supporting the \lstinline{lock} and \lstinline{unlock} methods. We develop a separation logic interface corresponding to \lstinline{BasicLockable} that is satisfied by all three of our mutex variants, and use it as a parameter to our RAII class specifications.

In summary, our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item Specifications of standard, recursive, and shared mutexes from the C++ standard library.
\item Implementations of each mutex type that are proven to satisfy our specifications, including some that do not satisfy the usual SL lock specifications.
\item A ghost-state library for thread identity tracking that we use to build the basic ownership predicates of the mutex specifications.
\item A generic interface for mutexes, corresponding to the \lstinline{BasicLockable} named requirement, and specifications for C++'s RAII objects that are parameterized by this interface.
\item A case study showing that thread-tracking predicates can be encapsulated inside an object, so that ownership of the object itself can be transferred between threads freely.
\end{itemize}

Our specifications and examples are implemented in BRiCk, but we expect that our formalisms can be reproduced in any Iris-based concurrent separation logic, whether theoretical (e.g., HeapLang) or realistic (e.g., RustBelt), once it has been augmented with thread-specific predicates. Object-oriented languages are the most direct application of the locking patterns we consider, particularly recursive mutexes, but non-OO languages such as C also have standard-library mutex implementations with the same thread restrictions (so our work could be usefully adapted to VST~\cite{vst}, for instance).

\section{Background}
\subsection{Lock Specifications in Separation Logic}
The standard specification of a lock in CSL associates each lock with a protected resource (sometimes called a \emph{lock invariant}, although we prefer to avoid overloading the word ``invariant'') that is gained when the lock is acquired and restored when it is released. The specifications are written as follows:
\[\begin{array}{c}
\{\ell \mapsto \mathsf{lock}(P)\}\ \texttt{lock}(\ell)\ \{\ell \mapsto \mathsf{lock}(P) \ast \mathsf{locked}(\ell) \ast P\}\vspace{.5em}\\
\{\ell \mapsto \mathsf{lock}(P) \ast \mathsf{locked}(\ell) \ast P\}\ \texttt{unlock}(\ell)\ \{\ell \mapsto \mathsf{lock}(P)\}
\end{array}\]
where $\mathsf{locked}(\ell)$ is a unique resource that can be held by at most one thread at a time.
\ignore{
In the atomic style, a lock is simply in one of two states, represented by e.g. a boolean that is $\mathsf{true}$ when the lock is held. Then acquire and release can be specified as:
\begin{mathpar}
\fforall b.\ \langle \ell \mapsto b \rangle\ \texttt{lock}(\ell)\ \langle \neg b \ast \ell \mapsto \mathsf{true} \rangle

\langle \ell \mapsto \mathsf{true} \rangle\ \texttt{unlock}(\ell)\ \langle \ell \mapsto \mathsf{false} \rangle
\end{mathpar}
While one thread is trying to acquire the lock, its state is unknown and may shift back and forth due to the behavior of other threads; at the lock's linearization point, we observe that the lock is not held ($\neg b$), and shift it to the held state ($\mathsf{true}$). By combining these specifications with a global invariant of the form $P \vee \ell \mapsto \mathsf{true}$, we can derive the invariant-style specs: an acquiring thread trades its ownership of the lock $\ell \mapsto \mathsf{true}$ for the invariant $P$, and then returns it before releasing the lock. (Less obviously, the TaDA-style specs can also be derived from invariant-style specs, using an invariant that is simply a ghost variable indicating the state $b$ of the lock%; see \citet{} for more details
.)}
These specifications capture the core idea of mutual exclusion, and can easily be shown to be satisfied by a simple implementation, such as a spinlock. They can also be used to verify very flexible synchronization patterns, such as the following \emph{daring concurrency} pattern:
\[\begin{array}{l || l}
\texttt{acquire(a);} & \texttt{acquire(b);}\\
\texttt{*x = *x + 1;} & \texttt{*x = *x + 1;}\\
\texttt{release(b);} & \texttt{release(a);}
\end{array}\]
In this program, each thread passes ownership of its lock to the other via another lock: if the left thread executes first, then when the second thread acquires \texttt{b} it also gains permission to release \texttt{a} (in the form of $\mathsf{locked}(a)$), and vice versa. Indeed, the ability to verify daring synchronization was one of the originally advertised strengths of concurrent separation logic~\cite{csl}.

However, the locks used in systems programming languages are not generally implemented this way, instead building on operating system primitives (e.g., Linux's futex~\cite{futex}) and highly optimized libraries (e.g., Pthread~\cite{pthread}) whose behavior depends on the thread holding the lock. This leads to both additional restrictions---e.g., locks may only be released by the thread that acquired them, or can only be deallocated if not held---and additional features---e.g., locks may be recursive, so that the holder can re-acquire them any number of times and only exits the critical section after performing an equal number of releases. In this paper, we show how to extend lock specifications to account for the restrictions and features of the mutexes in C++'s standard library.

\subsection{The BRiCk Logic for C++}
\label{brick}

\newcommand{\currentthread}[1]{\ensuremath{\mathtt{tid}(#1)}}

BRiCk~\cite{brick} is an Iris-based program logic for C++, inspired by Iris's HeapLang and the Verified Software Toolchain's logic for C~\cite{vst}. Its predicates and rules are similar to those of standard Iris instances, with special support for object-oriented data and templates. %anything else of note?
Unlike most Iris instances, it does not carry an adequacy proof that connects its rules to an operational semantics (indeed, there is no complete operational semantics for C++); it is an axiomatic semantics in the traditional sense. Its rules are justified by comparison to the (proved-sound) rules of HeapLang and VST, and by compiling and running example programs and checking that their behavior matches their specifications. BRiCk has been primarily used to verify low-level systems code, including the NOVA microkernel and applications on top of it~\cite{brick-os}.

One feature of BRiCk that is particularly relevant to our work is thread-specific predicates. In ordinary separation logic, all predicates can be transfered between threads: if thread $t_1$ owns $x \mapsto v$ and then synchronizes with $t_2$ via a lock or atomic operation, then afterwards $t_2$ may own $x \mapsto v$. This is problematic when the behavior of a function depends on the calling thread. BRiCk solves this using Iris's \emph{monotonic predicates}, previously used in weak-memory logics~\cite{igps} %and others
. Every BRiCk predicate is implicitly indexed by a thread ID, and a predicate $\currentthread{t}$ asserts that the current thread's ID is $t$. All other primitive predicates, such as memory ownership, are \emph{objective} and can be freely transferred between threads. This allows us to specify the fact that, e.g., a C++ \lstinline{mutex} can only be released by the thread that acquired it.

\input{specs.tex}

\section{RAII Lock Classes}

\newcommand{\lguard}[0]{\ensuremath{\mathsf{lguard}}}
\newcommand{\ulock}[0]{\ensuremath{\mathsf{ulock}}}

Managing locks manually is error-prone: it is easy to write code that acquires the same lock twice, forgets to release a lock, or releases a lock that has not been acquired. The Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII) pattern avoids these problems by connecting lock ownership to the lifetime of an object: the lock is acquired when the object is created and released when the object is destroyed, thus enjoying the guarantees of the language's memory management (an object will only be created and destroyed once each, will only be destroyed after it is created, will eventually be destroyed if unused, etc.). In this section we give specifications for two\footnote{In our Rocq development we also specify \lstinline{scoped_lock}, which takes a list of locks and acquires/releases them in an order guaranteed to avoid deadlock, but because we are working in a partial-correctness logic these specifications are not any more complicated and we do not discuss them here.} of the C++ standard library's RAII lock classes, \lstinline{lock_guard} and \lstinline{unique_lock}, and show how they build on our mutex specifications. %Their basic specifications are simple: the object's constructor has the same specification as the underlying lock's \lstinline{lock} method, and the destructor has the same specification as the underlying \lstinline{unlock}. The \lstinline{unique_lock} adds some complexity by allowing the user to manually acquire, release, and change the lock associated with the object.
The standard library implementations of \lstinline{lock_guard} and \lstinline{unique_lock} are simple enough that we were able to verify them directly against our specifications.

\subsection{Generic \lstinline{lock} and \lstinline{unlock}}
\label{basic-lockable}
The \lstinline{BasicLockable} named requirement describes the common interface
of types that provide \lstinline{lock()} and \lstinline{unlock()}
operations~\cite{ISO:2024:IIP}.  An invocation of \lstinline{lock()} blocks
until the calling thread acquires the lock, and \lstinline{unlock()} releases a
lock owned by the calling thread.  The caller must not already own the lock
when invoking \lstinline{lock()}, and must own it when invoking
\lstinline{unlock()}.  This is not a concrete class but a requirement on types: all the mutex classes implement it, and
user-defined lock types can as well.  Classes that are generic over a \lstinline{BasicLockable}
can operate on any such implementation.

We represent an implementation of \lstinline{BasicLockable} by a predicate
$R(q,m)$ describing fractional ownership $q$ of a lock with abstract state
$m$, together with two predicates $\dolock{p}{m}{K}$ and $\dounlock{p}{m}{K}$.
These predicates
describe the resources required to lock/unlock the object at pointer $p$ and produce the
the postcondition $K$ afterwards, in the predicate transformer style.  The generic specifications of \lstinline{lock} and \lstinline{unlock} are:
\[\begin{array}{c}    \{p\mapsto R(q,m)\ast \dolock{p}{m}{K}\}\ \texttt{p.lock()}\ \{p\mapsto R(q,m)\ast K\}\vspace{.5em}\\
\{p\mapsto R(q,m)\ast \dounlock{p}{m}{K}\}\ \texttt{p.unlock()}\ \{p\mapsto R(q,m)\ast K\}
\end{array}\]
The representation predicate is preserved by both operations, while the
implementation-specific predicates describe the change in ownership.
For example, the \lstinline{std::mutex} instance defines $\mathsf{do\_lock}$ to exchange the
calling thread's $\mathsf{not\_locked}$ predicate for the protected resource and the $\mathsf{m\_locked}$ predicate, and $\mathsf{do\_unlock}$ to perform the reverse exchange.  The
recursive and shared mutexes instantiate the same interface with their own
predicates.  Thus clients can use the two generic specifications without
depending on the particular mutex representation.

\subsection{\lstinline{std::lock_guard}}
\begin{figure}[htb]
\begin{lstlisting}
  std::mutex m;
  int size;

  bool get_size() {
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m);
    return size;
  }
\end{lstlisting}
\caption{A simple use of \lstinline{std::lock_guard} with a \lstinline{mutex}}
\label{lock-guard-ex}
\end{figure}

The \lstinline{lock_guard} class C++'s basic RAII class, a container for a single lock. It is a templated class that takes an arbitrary \lstinline{BasicLockable} class as an argument, acquires it when constructed, and releases it when destroyed. A simple example of its use is shown in Figure~\ref{lock-guard-ex}. The mutex \lstinline{m} is meant to protect the value of \lstinline{size}, and the \lstinline{lock_guard} object \lstinline{lock} in \lstinline{get_size} takes the place of calls to \lstinline{lock} and \lstinline{unlock}; \lstinline{m} is \lstinline{lock}ed at line 5 and \lstinline{unlock}ed after reading \lstinline{size} but before \lstinline{get_size} returns.

The \lstinline{lock_guard} class is parameterized by a \lstinline{BasicLockable} and class, our specification is likewise parameterized, calling $\mathsf{do\_lock}$ on creation and $\mathsf{do\_unlock}$ on destruction:
\[\begin{array}{c}
\{p \mapsto R(q, m) \ast \dolock{p}{m}{K}\}\ \texttt{lock\_guard(p)}\ \{g.\ g \mapsto \lguard(p, q, m) \ast K\} \vspace{.5em}\\
\{g \mapsto \lguard(p, q, m) \ast \dounlock{p}{m}{K}\}\}\ \texttt{g.}\!\!\sim\!\texttt{lock\_guard}()\ \{K \ast p \mapsto R(q, m)\}
\end{array}\]

\subsection{\lstinline{std::unique_lock}}
The \lstinline{unique_lock} class offers a more sophisticated RAII interface: the lock can be acquired and released manually as well as at construction/destruction, and the \lstinline{unique_lock} can be detached from one lock and attached to another during its lifetime. A \lstinline{unique_lock} object tracks whether it has acquired its associated mutex (if any), counting the acquisition from the constructor as well as explicit \lstinline{lock}/\lstinline{unlock} calls, and its destructor releases the mutex only if it is not currently acquired. %None of these operations are very complicated, but their specifications do need to account for many variations (no associated lock, associated lock is locked, associated lock is unlocked). %example?

The \lstinline{unique_lock} class has many constructors and operators; we specify a small set here, and more in our Rocq development. The abstract state of a \lstinline{unique_lock} is a tuple $(b, p, q, m)$, where $(p, q, m)$ is the associated mutex and $b$ is its state ($\mathsf{true}$ if held, $\mathsf{false}$ if not held).
%how much of this detail is useful? There are a lot of variations.
\[\begin{array}{c}%consider removing some newlines
\{p \mapsto R(q, m) \ast \dolock{p}{m}{K}\}\\ \texttt{unique\_lock(p)}\\ \{u.\ u \mapsto \ulock(\mathsf{true}, p, q, m) \ast K\} \vspace{1em}\\
\{p \mapsto R(q, m)\}\\ \texttt{unique\_lock(p, std::defer\_lock\_t)}\\ \{u.\ u \mapsto \ulock(\mathsf{false}, p, q, m)\} \vspace{1em}\\
\{u \mapsto \ulock(\mathsf{false}, p, q, m)\ast \dolock{p}{m}{K}\}\\ {\texttt{u.lock()}} \\ \{m \mapsto \ulock(\mathsf{true}, p, q, m) \ast K\}  \vspace{1em}\\
    \{u \mapsto \ulock(\mathsf{true}, p, q, m) \ast \dounlock{p}{m}{K}\}\\ {\texttt{u.unlock}()}\\
    \{m \mapsto \ulock(\mathsf{false}, p, q, m) \ast K\}  \vspace{1em} \\
\{u \mapsto \ulock(b, p, q, m) \ast (\text{if } b \text{ then } \dounlock{p}{m}{K} \text{ else } K)\}\\ \texttt{u.}\!\!\sim\!\texttt{unique\_lock}()\\ \{K \ast p \mapsto R(q, m)\}
\end{array}\]
The default constructor acquires the mutex $p$, so it needs $\dolock{p}{m}{K}$ in the precondition and creates a $\mathsf{ulock}$ in the $\mathsf{true}$ state. There is also a constructor that takes the \lstinline{std::defer_lock_t} argument and does not acquire the mutex, creating a $\mathsf{ulock}$ in the $\mathsf{false}$ state. When a \lstinline{unique_lock} is destroyed, it releases the underlying mutex only if it was in the $\mathsf{true}$ (held) state.

%move this to lock_guard?
\begin{figure}[htb]
\begin{lstlisting}[escapeinside    = {(*@}{@*)}]
  int val = 0;
  std::recursive_mutex m{};

  (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast \acquirable{N, \gamma}{t}{n}{q}{\lambda v.\,\texttt{val} \mapsto v}{x} \}$ @*)
  void inc() {
    std::unique_lock<std::recursive_mutex> lk(m);
    (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast \texttt{lk} \mapsto \ulock(\mathsf{true}, m, q, P) \ast \acquirable{N, \gamma}{t}{n+1}{q}{\lambda v.\,\texttt{val} \mapsto v}{x}\} \Rightarrow$ @*)
    (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast \texttt{lk} \mapsto \ulock(\mathsf{true}, m, q, P) \ast \texttt{val} \mapsto x \ast (\forall y.\,\texttt{val} \mapsto y \wand \acquirable{N, \gamma}{t}{n+1}{q}{\lambda v.\,\texttt{val} \mapsto v}{y})\}$ @*)
    val++;
    (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast \texttt{lk} \mapsto \ulock(\mathsf{true}, m, q, P) \ast \acquirable{N, \gamma}{t}{n+1}{q}{\lambda v.\,\texttt{val} \mapsto v}{x + 1}\}$ @*)
  }
  (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast \acquirable{N, \gamma}{t}{n}{q}{\lambda v.\,\texttt{val} \mapsto v}{x + 1})\}$ @*)

  (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast \acquirable{N, \gamma}{t}{n}{q}{\lambda v.\,\texttt{val} \mapsto v}{x} \}$ @*)
  void answer() {
    std::unique_lock<std::recursive_mutex> lk(m);
    (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast \texttt{lk} \mapsto \ulock(\mathsf{true}, m, q, P) \ast \acquirable{N, \gamma}{t}{n+1}{q}{\lambda v.\,\texttt{val} \mapsto v}{x}\} \Rightarrow$ @*)
    (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast \texttt{lk} \mapsto \ulock(\mathsf{true}, m, q, P) \ast \texttt{val} \mapsto x \ast (\forall y.\,\texttt{val} \mapsto y \wand \acquirable{N, \gamma}{t}{n+1}{q}{\lambda v.\,\texttt{val} \mapsto v}{y})\}$ @*)
    val = 41;
    (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast \texttt{lk} \mapsto \ulock(\mathsf{true}, m, q, P) \ast \acquirable{N, \gamma}{t}{n+1}{q}{\lambda v.\,\texttt{val} \mapsto v}{41})\}$ @*)
    inc();
    (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast \texttt{lk} \mapsto \ulock(\mathsf{true}, m, q, P) \ast \acquirable{N, \gamma}{t}{n+1}{q}{\lambda v.\,\texttt{val} \mapsto v}{42}\}$ @*)
  }
  (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast \acquirable{N, \gamma}{t}{n}{q}{\lambda v.\,\texttt{val} \mapsto v}{42} \}$ @*)
\end{lstlisting}
\caption{A program with multiple \lstinline{unique_lock}s around a single \lstinline{recursive_mutex}}
\label{unique-recursive}
\end{figure}
As discussed in Section~\ref{basic-lockable}, the \lstinline{BasicLockable} requirement does not explicitly require that \lstinline{lock} be mutual exclusive, and indeed recursive mutexes can be \lstinline{lock}ed multiple times without being \lstinline{unlock}ed. Thus, while each \lstinline{lock_guard} or \lstinline{unique_lock} object can only acquire its mutex at most once, we can construct multiple objects around a single recursive mutex, each of which manages a single acquisition.
The code in Figure~\ref{unique-recursive} shows how this can be used. When \lstinline{answer} is called, it acquires the recursive mutex \lstinline{m} by constructing a \lstinline{unique_lock} around it; it then calls \lstinline{inc}, which constructs another \lstinline{unique_lock} that acquires \lstinline{m} a second time. When each method returns, its \lstinline{unique_lock} is destroyed and \lstinline{m} is released once, so that \lstinline{m} is no longer locked after \lstinline{answer} returns.

Our specifications can be used to verify this program. When \lstinline{inc} constructs its \lstinline{unique_lock} around \lstinline{m}, it uses the $\mathsf{do\_lock}$ transformer of \lstinline{recursive_mutex} to determine its pre- and postcondition, incrementing the $\mathsf{holds}$ predicate's count by 1. Because $n + 1 > 0$, we can then borrow the protected resources, in this case $\texttt{val} \mapsto x$, from $\mathsf{holds}$, and restore them after running \lstinline{val++} with an argument value of $x + 1$. The \lstinline{unique_lock} destructor then calls the $\mathsf{do\_unlock}$ transformer, restoring the $\mathsf{holds}$ count to $n$. In \lstinline{answer}, we go through a similar process, incrementing the $\mathsf{holds}$ count and borrowing $\texttt{val}$ to set it to 41, but we then call \lstinline{inc} with the resulting predicate $\acquirable{N, \gamma}{t}{n+1}{q}{\lambda v.\,\texttt{val} \mapsto v}{41})$. This works exactly as desired: \lstinline{inc} acquires \lstinline{m} again with its \lstinline{unique_lock} and increments the hold count to $n + 2$, changes the argument from 41 to 42, and then releases \lstinline{m}, returning $\acquirable{N, \gamma}{t}{n+1}{q}{\lambda v.\,\texttt{val} \mapsto v}{42}$. Finally, \lstinline{answer}'s \lstinline{unique_lock} is destroyed, decrementing the count to the original $n$ and leaving us with the argument value of 42. Because our $\mathsf{do\_lock}$/$\mathsf{do\_unlock}$ interface makes no assumptions about the underlying mutex, we have no trouble verifying programs that construct multiple RAII objects around a single recursive mutex.

\section{Case Study: Mutex Encapsulation}
%\input{ring_buffer.tex}
%TODO: find or make some interesting examples

We have seen that enforcing the requirements of C++ mutexes requires the management of thread-specific permission predicates that are exchanged between threads and locks. We have demonstrated this approach in simple examples of each mutex type; we now consider whether our approach is modular enough to scale to larger programs. In Section~\ref{mutex-spec}, we explained that each mutex is given a user-chosen namespace $N$. In this section, we show how this approach lets us 1) demonstrate that two separate mutexes are indeed distinct, allowing a thread to acquire both of them at once, and 2) register and unregister threads as needed inside object methods, instead of requiring threads to hold on to non-transferable $\mathsf{not\_locked}$ predicates.
%There are at least two possible pitfalls. First, it might be difficult for a thread to acquire two different mutexes, because we need to manually prove that the second mutex is not the same as the first. Second and more subtly, thread-specific predicates might leak through layers of abstraction. Our mutex specifications must include predicates like $\notlocked{\gamma}{t}$ that explicitly mention thread IDs, but a data structure that uses a mutex internally should not need to expose thread IDs in its interface; it should be possible to share the data structure among threads exactly as one would a non-mutex-based implementation, without extra registration steps. In this section, we verify a case study showing that we avoid both these pitfalls, suggesting that our mutex specifications can indeed be used for modular verification.

\begin{figure}[htb]
\begin{lstlisting}
class Account {
private:
  unsigned long balance;
  std::recursive_mutex mut; // protects balance

public:
  explicit Account(unsigned long initial_balance) : balance(initial_balance) {}

  void incr_balance(unsigned long i) {
    std::lock_guard<std::recursive_mutex> lg(mut);
    balance += i;
  }

  void transfer_to(Account target, unsigned long i) {
    std::lock_guard<std::recursive_mutex> lg(mut);
    balance -= i;
    target.incr_balance(i);
  }
}

int main() {
  Account from{4};
  Account to{2};
  from.transfer_to(to, 3);
}
\end{lstlisting}
\caption{The code of our case study}
\label{transfer}
\end{figure}


The code of our case study is shown in Figure~\ref{transfer}. Each object of class \lstinline{Account} has a \lstinline{balance} protected by a mutex (in this code we use a \lstinline{recursive_mutex}, but any form of mutex would work). %make generic?
The \lstinline{transfer_to} method decrements the receiver's %terminology?
balance and increments the target object's balance, acquiring both mutexes in the process. Our questions are then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item How do we prove that we can acquire \lstinline{target}'s mutex, given that we already hold the receiver's mutex?
\item Can we use a representation predicate for \lstinline{Account} that does not include any thread-specific predicates and thus is freely transferable between threads?
\end{enumerate}

For question 2, recall that our specifications for \lstinline{recursive_mutex} are:
\[\begin{array}{c}
\{\currentthread{t} \ast m \mapsto_\pi \rmutex{N, \gamma}{P}\ast\acquirable{\gamma}{t}{n}{q}{P}{a}\}\\ {\texttt{m.lock()}} \\ \{\currentthread{t} \ast m \mapsto_\pi \rmutex{N, \gamma}{P}\ast \exists a'.\ \mathsf{acquire}(n, a, a') \ast \acquirable{N}{t}{n+1}{q}{P}{a'}\}  \vspace{1em}\\
    \{\currentthread{t} \ast m \mapsto_\pi \rmutex{N, \gamma}{P}\ast\acquirable{\gamma}{t}{n+1}{q}{P}{a}\}\\ {\texttt{m.unlock}()}\\
    \{\currentthread{t} \ast m \mapsto_\pi \rmutex{N, \gamma}{P}\ast\acquirable{\gamma}{t}{n}{q}{P}{a}\}
\end{array}\]
The $\mathsf{holds}$ predicate takes a thread $t$ that must match the current thread, and we must have it at line 15 %%confirm
in order to acquire \lstinline{mut}. On the other hand, \lstinline{transfer_to} is a function that can be called by any thread that has access to the two accounts involved, and should have a specification like
\[ \{ a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A \ast b \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_B \}\ \texttt{a.transfer\_to(b, n)}\ \{ a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A \ast b \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_B \}\]
In particular, if $\mathsf{account}$ takes a thread $t$ as an argument, then we will not be able to freely transfer ownership of it between threads (since it would only be usable by that thread $t$). The mutex permission library allows us to isolate this thread-local information. 

The representation predicate for \lstinline{Account} is defined as
\[p \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_N \triangleq \exists \gamma.\ p.\texttt{mut} \mapsto_q \rmutex{N, \gamma}{\lambda n.\ p.\texttt{balance} \mapsto n} \ast \mathsf{token}_\gamma(q) %can we get away with this quantification?
\]
Ownership of an \lstinline{Account} is simply ownership of the mutex protecting the \lstinline{balance} field plus a fraction of the mutex's $\mathsf{token}$. In particular, it makes no mention of a thread $t$ or the $\mathsf{holds}$ predicate. When we create an \lstinline{Account} we choose a namespace $N$ for it, which in turn is used as the namespace of its mutex field \lstinline{mut}. Inside \lstinline{incr_balance} and \lstinline{transfer_to}, we register the calling thread with $N$, %recap the registration rule
acquire \lstinline{mut}, release \lstinline{mut} at the end of the method, and then unregister the thread. Registration requires both $\mutexperm{}{N}$ and $\token{N, \gamma}{q}$; the latter is part of $\mathsf{account}$, while the former is passed separately. Concretely, the specification we use for \lstinline{incr_balance} is:
\[\begin{array}{c}
\{ a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A \ast \mutexperm{t}{A} \ast \currentthread{t} \} \\ \texttt{a.incr\_balance(i)}\\ 
\{ a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A \ast \mutexperm{t}{A} \ast \currentthread{t} \} \end{array}\]
and the specification for \lstinline{transfer_to} is:
\[\begin{array}{c}\{ a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A \ast b \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_B \ast \mutexperm{t}{A} \ast \mutexperm{t}{B} \ast \currentthread{t} \}\\ \texttt{a.transfer\_to(b, n)}\\ \{ a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A \ast b \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_B  \ast \mutexperm{t}{A} \ast \mutexperm{t}{B} \ast \currentthread{t} \}
\end{array}\]
By choosing distinct namespaces $A \neq B$ for the two accounts (and thus their mutexes), we can easily obtain $\mutexperm{t}{A} \ast \mutexperm{t}{B}$ from a thread's starting $\mutexperm{t}{\top}$. The full proof outline for the example is shown in Figure~\ref{transfer-proof}.

\begin{figure}[htb]
\begin{lstlisting}[escapeinside    = {(*@}{@*)}]
class Account {
private:
  unsigned long balance;
  std::recursive_mutex mut; // protects balance

public:
  (*@ $\{ \mathsf{emp} \}$ @*)
  explicit Account(unsigned long initial_balance) : balance(initial_balance) {}
  (*@ $\{ a.\ a \mapsto \mathsf{account}_N \}$ @*)

  (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A \ast \mutexperm{t}{A}  \}$ @*)
  void incr_balance(unsigned long i) {
    (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast a.\texttt{mut} \mapsto_q \rmutex{A, \gamma}{\lambda n.\,p.\texttt{balance} \mapsto n} \ast \mathsf{token}_\gamma(q) \ast \mutexperm{t}{A} \} \Rightarrow$ @*) 
    (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast a.\texttt{mut} \mapsto_q \rmutex{A, \gamma}{\lambda n.\,p.\texttt{balance} \mapsto n} \ast \notlocked{N, \gamma}{t}{q} \}$ @*) 
    std::lock_guard<std::recursive_mutex> lg(mut);
    balance += i;
    (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast a.\texttt{mut} \mapsto_q \rmutex{A, \gamma}{\lambda n.\ p.\texttt{balance} \mapsto n} \ast \notlocked{A, \gamma}{t}{q} \} \Rightarrow$ @*)
    (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast a.\texttt{mut} \mapsto_q \rmutex{A, \gamma}{\lambda n.\ p.\texttt{balance} \mapsto n} \ast \mathsf{token}_A(q) \ast \mutexperm{t}{A} \}$ @*)
  }
  (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t} \ast a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A \ast \mutexperm{t}{A}\}$ @*)

  void transfer_to(Account target, unsigned long i) { %%needs outline
    std::lock_guard<std::recursive_mutex> lg(mut);
    balance -= i;
    target.incr_balance(i);
  }
}

int main() {
  (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t_0} \ast \mutexperm{t_0}{\top} \}$ @*)
  Account from{4};
  Account to{2};
  (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t_0} \ast \mutexperm{t_0}{\top} \ast a \mapsto \mathsf{account}_A \ast b \mapsto \mathsf{account}_B \} \Rightarrow$ @*)
  (*@ $\{ \currentthread{t_0} \ast \mutexperm{t_0}{\top \setminus A \setminus B} \ast \mutexperm{t_0}{A} \ast \mutexperm{t_0}{B} \ast a \mapsto \mathsf{account}_A \ast b \mapsto \mathsf{account}_B \}$ @*)
  from.transfer_to(to, 3);
}
\end{lstlisting}
\caption{The proof outline of our case study}
\label{transfer-proof}
\end{figure}

More complex synchronization patterns may have to expose locked states (and thus thread-specific predicates) their clients, but when objects always return to the client in an unlocked state, the thread-specific predicates can be handled internally and do not affect the representation predicate: instead, each thread separately manages its set of namespaces, and any thread that is not already using the object's namespace may call its methods. In this case, the predicate $a \mapsto_q \mathsf{account}_A$ can be transferred to any other thread, and that thread can call $a$'s methods as long as it is not currently holding a mutex with the namespace $A$. Namespaces are chosen arbitrarily during verification, so we can always choose a unique name for $A$ and allow any thread to use $a$. %make this more precise

\section{Proof Methods and AI}
All specifications and proofs were developed in Rocq using BRiCk. We developed the specifications manually, then used AI tools to refactor the specifications and generate some of the proofs.

\section{Related Work}
The most closely related work is that of \citet{vercors-reentrant}, who gave SL specifications for reentrant (i.e., recursive) locks in Java in the VerCors logic; these specifications were later generalized to non-reentrant and reader-writer locks~\cite{vercors-locks}. They extended their logic with a primitive \emph{lockset} predicate for each thread that records the list of mutexes currently held by the thread (i.e., the inverse of our $\mutexperm{t}{A}$). The lockset predicate is monolithic and cannot be split or joined, nor can it be transferred between threads, and to support proving that a newly created lock is not in the lockset, their postcondition for the lock constructor explicitly states that the newly created lock is distinct from all previously allocated objects. They also have two separate proof rules for first and repeated acquires, and likewise for release. The lockset cannot be transferred between threads because lock invariants in VerCors are not impredicative, i.e., it is not possible to pass arbitrary resources between threads. In fact, the authors discuss the possibility of a counting $\mathsf{holds}$ predicate like ours, but conclude that it is impossible because they have no way to share it between threads. In contrast, our approach builds lock permissions out of an arbitrary ghost state construction in an impredicative logic and allows them to be passed between threads like any other predicate; the only extension to the logic we require is the presence of the thread-specific $\currentthread{t}$ predicate (which can be defined using the monotonic-predicate construction). We also give a single, intuitive specification for recursive lock acquire/release in terms of the $\mathsf{holds}$ predicate%, using the borrowing approach to solve the problem of acquiring the protected resources twice
.

BRiCk is one of a family of tools that apply CSL to real programming languages. The Verified Software Toolchain (VST)~\cite{vst} targets C code with CSL specifications directly, and RustBelt~\cite{rustbelt} does the same for Rust. RefinedC~\cite{refinedc} and RefinedRust~\cite{refinedrust} instead use semi-automatically checkable ownership type systems that are backed by CSL reasoning. All of these systems have been used to verify lock implementations and clients, but all of their lock specifications are in the usual CSL style and do not track thread IDs.

Standard libraries are an appealing target for verification since they are widely used, but relatively few projects have aimed to comprehensively verify them. The JaVerT toolchain for JavaScript verification~\cite{javert} implemented a large fraction of the JavaScript standard libraries and gave CSL specifications for them, covering many built-in data structures and types as well as fundamental object-oriented features. \citet{cakeml-io} verified a file I/O library in CakeML. \citet{irc11-rcu} verified an RCU implementation in the weak-memory iRC11 logic, which could serve as a starting point for the RCU features added in C++26. Most recently, \citet{rust-stdlib} reported on a massive open-source effort to prove safety of the Rust standard library, accepting proofs from a range of tools with varying guarantees. This effort included a VeriFast verification of a (basic) mutex implementation; in Rust the same thread acquiring a mutex twice may crash the program but is not undefined behavior, so this specification did not require $\mathsf{not\_locked}$-style predicates. Rust's standard library does not currently include a recursive mutex, but one has been proposed for inclusion, so future versions of the library may also benefit from our approach.

\section{Conclusion and Future Work}
While locks are widely used in concurrent separation logic, in many concurrent programming languages the standard CSL lock specs only accurately describe the behavior of inefficient implementations (e.g., spinlocks). More idiomatic and efficient mutex implementations such as Pthread make use of OS primitives that record and place restrictions on the threads accessing the mutex. We have demonstrated that these restrictions can be captured in separation logic specifications, through the combination of a fractional token and a system of per-thread mutex tracking, and that these features can be implemented with standard Iris ghost state plus a simple thread-specific predicate. This lets us give accurate specifications for basic, recursive, and shared mutexes from the C++ standard library, as well as the RAII classes that wrap these mutexes. Our specifications require additional mutex-tracking reasoning that is not needed when using naive lock specifications, but this reasoning is relatively simple to discharge and can be encapsulated, so that the client of an object with an internal mutex needs only reserve the object's namespace and does not need to directly reason about mutexes or thread-specific predicates.

C++'s thread support library includes many other concurrency primitives, such as condition variables (which allow more efficient mutex management), futures (which encapsulate asynchronous computations), and, as of the recent C++26 revision, RCU wrappers (for efficient concurrent memory reclamation). We are interested in extending our work to faithful specifications of these more sophisticated concurrency primitives. We are also interested in proving that our specifications are met by real standard-library mutex implementations (e.g., the Pthread mutex), which will require formalizing the interface provided by OS primitives such as \lstinline{futex}. %more
Ultimately, through careful attention to the informal specifications and existing implementations of standard libraries, we aim to bring the theory of concurrent separation logic to bear on real-world concurrent programs.

\section{Data-Availability Statement}
All specifications and proofs in the paper are formalized in Rocq using BRiCk. Our proofs and the rules of BRiCk's logic are open-source, but its automation is proprietary and is needed to run our proofs. We will make an artifact available in the form of anonymous remote access to a machine with access to the BRiCk automation.
